## Overview

This session has two parts. First, a brief introduction to **off-policy evaluation** (OPE) — how to estimate what a learned policy *would* have achieved using historical data, without deploying it. Second, **Jigsaw 4**, our structured discussion of four applied policy learning papers. Expert groups share what they learned, teaching groups synthesize across papers, and we close with a whole-class discussion on when policy learning actually works in practice — and when it fails.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

1. Define off-policy evaluation and explain why it's hard
2. Distinguish the three main OPE estimators (direct, IPW, doubly-robust) and describe when each breaks
3. Explain how the papers in Jigsaw 4 apply policy learning to real health settings
4. Critique a published policy learning application — identify what the authors did well, what they glossed over, and what you'd push back on
5. Articulate the recurring tensions in applied policy learning: interpretability vs. optimality, efficiency vs. equity, single-outcome vs. multi-outcome

### The Four Papers

1. **Bodory, Mascolo & Lechner (2024)** — Policy trees on the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment (applied, Medicaid)
2. **Cerulli, Ferro & Ferretti (2024)** — Multi-outcome anti-malarial subsidy targeting in Kenya
3. **Stijven et al. (2025)** — Optimal treatment regimes in a real depression RCT (practical challenges)
4. **Viviano & Bradic (2024)** — Fair policy targeting and the efficiency–equity Pareto frontier
